newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Bankers Trust urges re-think of NZ pension debate.
newsitem.headline: Bankers Trust urges re-think of NZ pension debate.

text.p: Bankers Trust NZ Ltd said on Tuesday that pension policy alternatives should be revisited before New Zealanders made a decision on private or public provision.
BTNZ said the debate had been derailed by "undue haste" and "blinkered policy development" and that it had failed to answer the question of what the country could afford.
The bank advocates the formation of a review team to assume a wider investigative brief to focus on economic sustainability.
Its brief would include all aspects of provision for retirement, both public and private.
BTNZ chief executive Rob Morrison said in a statement fundamental economic issues had been brushed aside in the rush for politicians and others to score quick political points.
Consensus could only achieved through considering the relevant facts.

"This has not been the policy development process we have observed in the last six months," he said. "Instead we have seen a knee-jerk reaction to meet an artificial deadline linked to the introduction of tax cuts in July next year," he said.

"The undue haste to introduce the compulsory retirement savings scheme, which pre-empted the first review of the Todd Task Force on superannuation, has ensured that no consensus can be achieved for this proposal," he said.

"Personal savings and taking responsibility for your own lifestyle in retirement should be an integral part of this framework, but it is premature to decide unilaterally that compulsion is the best way forward," he said.
A "no" vote in September's referendum would present the opportunity for a more measured approach to any future proposal.

BTNZ chief economist David Plank told a news conference the current proposal simply shifted the onus for retirement income from the public sector to the private sector with provision for government topups. "This may lower the cost to the government but it does not necessarily ensure sustainability," he said.

"We need to shift away from a narrow focus on fiscal resonsiblity and government expenditure to one which addresses the wider issue of what is economically sustainable for the economy as a whole," he said.
Plank said BTNZ was also concerned that there did not appear to be a "plan B" in place if the referendum fails.

Another fault in the policy-making process was that there was little consensus among the political parties. This, together with a low turnout in September, could mean more changes further down the track, BTNZ said.
